source_text: ἐπαρκοῦντες δεομένοις, καὶ τὰ ἐφ' οἷς ἂν ἥδοιτο Θεὸς, ἀποπεραίνειν εὖ μάλα διεσπουδακότες. Ἆρ' οὐ διφυής ἐστί πως τῆς δικαιοσύνης ὁ τρόπος, εἴς τε ἡμᾶς αὐτοὺς, καὶ μέν τοι καὶ εἰς ἑτέρους κατορθούμενος; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ἔοικε. {ΚΥΡ.} Ὁπλῇ δὴ οὖν ἐσχισμένῃ, ἤτοι ποδὸς διχηλίᾳ, παρεικάζει πως ἀεὶ τὸν τοιοῦτον ὁ νόμος. Ποῦς γὰρ ἀεὶ, πορείας μὲν ἡμῖν τῆς κατ' ἐνέργειαν πρακτικῆς σύμβολον ἂν εἴη καὶ τύπος· καὶ δή φαμεν, ὀρθῷ διάττειν ποδὶ, τοὺς ἀμωμήτως ἰέναι πρὸς τὸ τελοῦν εἰς ὄνησιν εὖ μάλα προθυμουμένους. Ἀναμέλπει δέ που καὶ ὁ Δαβίδ· «Ὁ γὰρ ποῦς μου ἔστη ἐν εὐθύτητι,» τοῦτ' ἔστιν, ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ πεπόρευμαι καὶ εὐθύτητι· μεμίσηκα δὲ τὸ διεστραμμένον. Περὶ δέ γε τῶν φιλαμαρτημόνων· «Ὀξεῖς οἱ πόδες αὐτῶν ἐκχέαι αἷμα, σύντριμμα δὲ καὶ ταλαιπωρία ἐν ταῖς ὁδοῖς αὐτῶν.» Οὐκοῦν τῆς μὲν ἐν ἔργοις πορείας σύμβολον ὁ ποῦς. Διχηλιὰ δέ γε τύπος ἂν εἴη σαφὴς τοῦ ἐπ' ἄμφω βαίνειν ἡμᾶς ὀρθῶς καὶ ἀνεπιπλήκτως δύνασθαι, εἰς τὸ καθ' ἡμᾶς αὐτοὺς, καὶ μέν τοι καὶ εἰς ἑτέρους. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Πιθανὸς ὁ λόγος. {ΚΥΡ.} Εἴ τις οὖν εἴη τυχὸν, ὀρθῶς καὶ ἐπιστημόνως ἐπ' ἄμφω βαίνειν εἰδὼς, ἑαυτόν τε καὶ ἑτέρους ὠφελεῖν οἷός τε, τῇ τῶν ἠθῶν ποιότητι λέγω, καὶ πρός γε δὴ τούτῳ, νουνεχὴς καὶ ἐμφρονέστατος, καὶ τοῖς περὶ Θεοῦ λόγοις ἐναύλιον ὥσπερ τι καὶ ἐνδιαίτημα διδοὺς τὴν καρδίαν, ἄνω τε καὶ κάτω στρέφων ἀείπως ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὰς τῶν θείων δογμάτων ἐννοίας, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο πυκνῶς καὶ ἐμφρόνως ἐξερευνᾷν, καταλεπτύνων τρόπον τινὰ τὰ οὕτω τῶν νοημάτων ἀκριβῶς ἐγνωσμένα, ζώῳ που πάντως ἔσται προσεοικὼς ἀναφέροντι τὸν μηρυκισμὸν, καὶ τὴν ἐν κοιλίᾳ τροφὴν ἀνερευγομένῳ ἀεὶ, καὶ τοῖς ὀδοῦσιν ὑπάγοντι, ὡς ἂν καὶ ἔτι καταλεαίνοιτο, καὶ τῷ τῆς πέψεως ἰσχνῷ χωροίη πρὸς ὄνησιν. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Εὖ λέγεις. {ΚΥΡ.} Καθαρὸν δὲ εἶναί φησι τὸ ζῶον, ὅπερ ἂν ἔχῃ πρὸς διχηλοῦσαν ὁπλὴν ἐκτελευτῶντα τὸν πόδα, ἀνακομίζει τε αὖ τὸν ἐν κοιλίᾳ μηρυκισμόν· ὁ γὰρ εἶναι πεφυκὼς ἄριστός τε καὶ ἀγαθὸς εἰς ἑαυτὸν καὶ ἑτέρους, προσειληφὼς δὲ καὶ τὸ φιλόλογον καὶ τὸ εἰς γνῶσιν ἐντριβὲς, δῆλον δὲ ὅτι τὴν ἐπὶ Θεῷ, ἄρτιος ἔσται πρὸς ἀρετὴν, καὶ ἀμωμήτως ἔχων ἔν γε τοῖς καθ' ἑαυτὸν, πρὸς πᾶν ὁτιοῦν τῶν τεθαυμασμένων· κἂν εἰ μέτοχός τις τοῦ τοιοῦδε γένοιτο τυχὸν, κατὰ μάθησιν λέγω, καὶ οἱονείπως καταθοινήσαιτο τὸν παρ' αὐτοῦ λόγον, κἂν εἰ γένοιτο μιμητὴς, ἕλοιτό τε ζηλοῦν τὸν ὧδε διαπρεπῆ καὶ ἐξαίρετον, ἀβέβηλος ἔσται καὶ καθαρός. Συνδιαιτήσεται γὰρ καθαρῷ, καὶ τῆς ἐν αὐτῷ συνέσεως καὶ χρηστομαθίας ἐκμαγεῖον ὥσπερ τι τὸν οἰκεῖον εὐθὺς ἀναδείξει τρόπον. Τοῦτο, οἶμαι, ἐστὶ τὸ δεῖν ἐσθίειν ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ παντὸς ζώου κατασχίζοντος φυσικῶς εἰς ὁπλὴν τὸν πόδα, καὶ ἀνάνον
pass_a_gloss: Cyr. (continuing the list from §17 of goods done toward brothers): supplying those in need, and being very eager to accomplish the things in which God would take pleasure. Is not the manner of righteousness somehow two-natured, set right both toward ourselves and toward others? Pall.: It seems. Cyr.: With a split hoof, that is, the cleaving of the foot, the law likens such a one. The foot would be a symbol and type of the practical journey by action; we say 'to go through with straight foot' of those eager to go blamelessly toward what ends in profit. David sings: 'my foot stood in uprightness', i.e. I walked in righteousness and uprightness and hated the perverted. Of sin-lovers: 'sharp their feet to pour out blood, crushing and misery in their ways'. So the foot = symbol of the journey in works; the cleaving = type of our being able to step on both rightly and unrebuked, toward ourselves and toward others. Pall.: Persuasive the word. Cyr.: If someone knows how to step on both rightly and knowingly, able to profit himself and others by quality of character, and besides sensible, most prudent, giving his heart as a lodging and dwelling to the words about God, turning up and down in himself the notions of divine doctrines, and so [knowing] to search out often and wisely, grinding fine the thoughts exactly known, he will resemble an animal bringing up rumination, always belching up the food in the belly and putting it under the teeth so that it may be ground smoother and by the fineness of digestion proceed to benefit. Pall.: You speak well. Cyr.: He says the animal is clean which has the foot ending in a cloven hoof and brings back the rumination in the belly; for the one naturally excellent and good to himself and others, having taken on love of learning and practice in knowledge, that is, of God, will be complete toward virtue, blameless in his own affairs, toward anything admired. And if one should partake of such a one by learning, and as it were feast on his word, and become an imitator, choosing to emulate one so distinguished, he will be unprofaned and clean; for he will live with a clean one and show his own manner as an impression of the understanding and good learning in him. This, I think, is the need for us to eat from every animal naturally splitting the foot into a hoof and bring[ing up] (text breaks -)…
pass_b_english: Cyril: …coming to the aid of those in need, and taking great pains to carry out whatever things God delights in. Is not the way of righteousness, then, in a sense twofold, since it is carried out both toward ourselves and toward others?

Cyril: The law, then, always likens such a person, in a way, to a parted hoof, that is, to a foot divided in two (Leviticus 11:3). For the foot would always be for us a symbol and type of the road we travel in practical action. Indeed we speak of those who are truly eager to go blamelessly toward what leads to their good as walking with a straight foot. David also sings somewhere: ‘For my foot has stood on level ground’ (Psalm 26:12), that is, I have walked in righteousness and uprightness, and I have hated what is crooked. And of those who love sin he says: ‘Their feet are swift to shed blood; ruin and misery are in their paths’ (Romans 3:15–16). So the foot is a symbol of the road we travel in deeds. And the parting of the hoof would be a clear type of our being able to walk rightly and beyond reproach in both ways: in what concerns ourselves, and also toward others.

Cyril: Suppose, then, there is someone who knows how to walk rightly and skillfully in both ways, and is able to benefit both himself and others (I mean by the quality of his character). Suppose that besides this he is sensible and very wise, and gives his heart to the words about God as a kind of lodging and dwelling place; that he is always turning over within himself, this way and that, the meanings of the divine doctrines, and so knows how to search them out often and wisely, grinding fine, as it were, the thoughts he has come to know so exactly. Such a person will surely resemble an animal that brings up the cud: it is always bringing back up the food in its belly and putting it under its teeth, so that it may be ground finer still and, made fine enough to digest, may turn to its benefit.

Cyril: Now the law says that an animal is clean if its foot ends in a parted hoof and it also brings back up the cud from its belly (Leviticus 11:3). For the one who is by nature excellent and good toward himself and toward others, and who has also taken on a love of learning and practice in knowledge (plainly, the knowledge of God), will be fully fitted for virtue and for every admirable thing, and blameless, at least in what concerns himself. And if someone comes to share in such a person (I mean by learning from him), and feasts, as it were, on the teaching he gives; if he becomes his imitator and chooses to emulate one so distinguished and outstanding, he will be undefiled and clean. For he will be living with one who is clean, and he will at once show his own way of life to be a kind of imprint of the understanding and sound learning found in that man. This, I think, is what is meant by our having to eat of every animal that by nature splits its foot at the hoof and brings up…

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of De adoratione Book 14 exists to compare. Translated fresh from the Migne PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the withheld earlier English was not used as a base.

apparatus.note: Migne PG 68 print; the column break may cut a sentence or a word.

Opens mid-sentence, completing Cyril's list of good works done toward others begun at the end of §17 (the §17 English should end on that list). 'For my foot has stood on level ground' is LXX Psalm 25:12, English Psalm 26:12 (εὐθύτης, 'uprightness' or 'level ground'). 'Their feet are swift to shed blood…' matches Romans 3:15–16 word for word (ὀξεῖς); Paul draws it from Isaiah 59:7–8, and some LXX manuscripts carry the same lines in Psalm 13:3 (English 14:3); Cyril's 'of those who love sin' may still be David speaking, but the wording follows Romans, so Romans is cited. The gloss 'I have hated what is crooked' is Cyril's own paraphrase, not cited. 'Walk with a straight foot' (ὀρθῷ ποδί) is a common Greek proverb, not Scripture; compare Galatians 2:14 (ὀρθοποδοῦσιν), uncited. 'Fully fitted… for every admirable thing' (ἄρτιος… πρὸς πᾶν) may echo 2 Timothy 3:17; doubtful, uncited. The infinitive ἐξερευνᾷν is taken as governed by εἰδώς ('knows how to search them out'). The section breaks inside a word, ἀνάνον|τος (§19); read ἀνάγοντος, the Leviticus 11:3 verb (ἀνάγον μηρυκισμόν); 'ἀνάνοντος' is not a Greek word and is likely a print or OCR slip. The citation for this last clause is placed at its end in §19.
proverb 'walk with a straight foot' taken out of quotation marks (not Scripture; avoids Scripture-quote voice) and 'very eager' (εὖ μάλα) restored
ἄρτιος... πρὸς πᾶν ὁτιοῦν τῶν τεθαυμασμένων re-attached to 'fully fitted' (was 'blameless with regard to every admirable thing')
Scripture checked: Psalm 26:12 (LXX 25:12) exact; Romans 3:15-16 exact wording (Isaiah 59:7-8 source); Leviticus 11:3 correct
